title: What Is CompuServe? — Definition
body:
The pre-web and early-web online world: ARPANET and its protocols, Usenet newsgroups, BBSes and Fidonet, Gopher, WAIS, Archie, dial-up ISPs (CompuServe, AOL, Prodigy), Mosaic and the browser wars, and the folk culture of the early web — Geocities neighborhoods, webrings, guestbooks, and 'under construction' GIFs.

In the context of this database, the CompuServe is presented as one internet history record among the early internet and online history family. 1979's commercial online: forums, email, and $12/hour — the professionals' network.

title: Origins and History of CompuServe
body:
The CompuServe belongs to the 1979–2009 era and traces to CompuServe (H&R Block).

ARPANET's first message (1969, 'LO' — the system crashed on 'LOGIN') grew into a research network; TCP/IP cutover was January 1, 1983. Usenet (1979) gave the world distributed discussion; BBSes (1978, Ward Christensen's CBBS) gave hobbyists dial-up community. Commercial services — CompuServe (1979), Prodigy, GEnie, AOL — sold walled gardens by the hour. Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web (1990–91) plus Mosaic (1993) made the internet visual and public; Netscape's 1995 IPO ignited the dot-com boom. Microsoft's Internet Explorer bundling sparked the browser wars and the 1998 antitrust case. By 2000 the web had absorbed everything — Gopher, BBS, and walled gardens faded into nostalgia.

Within that longer story, CompuServe: The CB simulator (1980) was the first online chat; GIF was invented here (1987). AOL bought it (1997); the classic service ended 2009.

title: How CompuServe Works
body:
Dial-up modems turned digital bits into audio tones over phone lines (300 to 56k baud); SLIP/PPP carried TCP/IP over the call. Usenet flooded articles server-to-server; NNTP clients read them like a global bulletin board. BBSes answered one phone line at a time — Fidonet echomail relayed messages nightly in the 'zone mail hour'. Gopher's menus and WAIS's search predated the web's hyperlinks; Archie indexed FTP sites. The web's HTTP/HTML/URL trio made every document addressable and clickable.

Applied to the CompuServe (1979–2009, CompuServe (H&R Block)): AOL bought it (1997); the classic service ended 2009.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of CompuServe — Components
body:
Every CompuServe is an assembly of the early internet and online history family's standard parts:

• Modem — Modulator-demodulator; the handshake screech is iconic.
• UART / serial port — The PC's link to the modem.
• Phone line — The original last mile; one line, one call.
• BBS software — RBBS, Fido, Wildcat, MajorBBS — the host programs.
• NNTP server — Usenet article store-and-forward.
• Gopher server — Menu-based document hierarchy on port 70.
• Web server — CERN httpd, NCSA HTTPd — HTTP on port 80.
• Browser — Mosaic, Netscape, IE: rendering HTML.
• ISP POP — Point of presence with modem banks and hunt groups.
• Newsgroup hierarchy — comp.*, sci.*, rec.*, alt.* — the topic tree.

When examining a surviving CompuServe, identify these parts in order: Modem, UART / serial port, Phone line, BBS software, NNTP server, Gopher server.

title: Early Internet and Online History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of early internet and online history:

• baud / bps — Modem speeds: 300, 1200, 2400, 9600, 14.4k, 28.8k, 33.6k, 56k.
• handshake — The screeching negotiation of speed and protocol.
• BBS — Bulletin Board System; one-line dial-up community.
• Fidonet — Amateur BBS network; nightly echomail exchanges.
• Usenet — Distributed newsgroups; 'the internet's original forum'.
• flame war — Heated newsgroup argument; Godwin's law was coined for them.
• spam — Named for the Monty Python sketch; first major spam: Canter & Siegel, 1994.
• netiquette — The social contract: no top-posting, lurk before posting.
• lurk — Reading without posting; encouraged for newcomers.
• webring — Linked circle of related sites; peak 1990s navigation.
• guestbook — Sign-here page; the social plugin of 1997.
• under construction — The animated GIF that adorned half the early web.

title: CompuServe in Culture
body:
The early internet was a frontier town: ASCII art, .plan files, 'you've got mail', modem symphonies, and the sacred 56k handshake. Usenet gave us FAQs, spoiler warnings, and eternal September (AOL's 1993 flood). Geocities neighborhoods had addresses like 'Area51/Dimension'. People built homepages by hand in Notepad, counted hits proudly, and signed every guestbook. It was smaller, weirder, and human-scaled.

The CompuServe carries that cultural charge directly: AOL bought it (1997); the classic service ended 2009.

title: Collecting and Preserving CompuServe
body:
Modems (Hayes Smartmodem, USR Courier) are the totems; boxed AOL trial disks are kitsch gold. BBS software disks, Usenet CD archives, and ISP install CDs are ephemera worth saving. Old routers (Cisco AGS) are furniture. Archive everything — magnetic media from the '90s is entering the danger zone.

For the CompuServe specifically: 1979's commercial online: forums, email, and $12/hour — the professionals' network.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working CompuServe with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: CompuServe Restoration Guide
body:
BBSes can be revived on emulators or real hardware with telnet front-ends (no more phone lines needed). Old browsers run in VMs; the Wayback Machine fills gaps. Document your configs — dial-up networking stacks are fiddly and knowledge is evaporating.

Restoration order for a CompuServe: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical internet history record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: CompuServe — UUCP bang-path + classful subnet demo (Runnable Python)
body:
Parses a 1980s UUCP bang-path email route and computes classful network ranges — addressing before the modern internet.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the CompuServe so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# UUCP bang-path routing + classful addressing (public-domain concepts)
import ipaddress

def route_bang_path(path):
    hops = path.split("!")
    user = hops.pop()
    print(f"To: {user}")
    for i, h in enumerate(hops):
        print(f"  hop {i+1}: {h} -> {'deliver to ' + user if i == len(hops)-1 else hops[i+1]}")

route_bang_path("seismo!mcvax!ukc!haro!user")
print()

# Classful networks, the pre-CIDR world (pre-1993)
for net in ["10.0.0.0/8", "172.16.0.0/16", "192.168.1.0/24"]:
    n = ipaddress.ip_network(net)
    cls = "A" if net.endswith("/8") else "B" if net.endswith("/16") else "C"
    print(f"Class {cls} {n}: {n.num_addresses} addresses, "
          f"host range {n.network_address+1} .. {n.broadcast_address-1}")
